tagline.text: A 24-hectare heritage campus founded in 1905 in Jaro, with a Christmas festival of lights

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Dec–Jan festival season, Nov–May dry season

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200~800 (estimated for transport and meals, per person for half a day)

children.text: Central Philippine University in Iloilo City's Jaro District is a 24-hectare campus that began in 1905 as the Jaro Industrial School. It has American-colonial-era buildings, a national historical marker, the UNESCO-inscribed Hinilawod recordings, and a festival of lights every December.

Central Philippine University (CPU) is a private university in Jaro District, Iloilo City. It began on October 1, 1905, when the American Baptist Foreign Mission Society opened the Jaro Industrial School. According to Wikipedia and the university's own history, its first principal was Rev. William O. Valentine, and it became Central Philippine School in 1923, Central Philippine College in 1936, and a university in 1953.

The campus sits on about 24 hectares between the Tigum River and Dungon Creek. According to the university's history page, the missionaries bought the land in 1904, when it was a sugarcane field with a distillery and a small sugar mill, and it had also been a battleground in the Philippine-American War, including the Battle of Sambag in 1899. Most buildings were destroyed in World War II, but six concrete structures survived: Valentine Hall, Lopez Hall, Franklin Hall, Roblee Hall, Weston Hall and the President's House. Classes resumed in July 1946.

The school's beginnings involved a gift from the American industrialist John D. Rockefeller. According to the university, in 1901 the American Baptist Foreign Mission Society received $2,000 from Rockefeller to start a school in the Philippines, and in 1904 it bought the site for about 9,000 pesos. The site was chosen for its nearness to a navigable river, the railroad and the main road. The NHCP marker records that this was the first Philippine school where students worked to pay for their education, and that it set up the country's first student government, the CPU Republic, in 1906. Today the campus is a Registered Cultural Property of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) and a Marked Historical Site of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP), and nine campus buildings are listed in the Philippine Registry of Heritage.

Some later history helps you read the buildings. In 1966 Rex D. Drilon became the first Filipino president, and according to the university, on December 25, 1969 the American Baptist Foreign Mission Society transferred the whole campus to CPU. In 1943, during World War II, missionaries were killed, so every building here is also a record of war and rebuilding. This is not a ticketed attraction but a working campus with more than 15,000 students. It suits a quiet walk on a weekday during the school term to see the old buildings and gardens, and during the festival of lights that starts in early December the night scenery becomes the main draw. It is close to Jaro Cathedral, so the two pair well.

blocks.title: Centennial Walkway and the NHCP marker

children.text: The Centennial Walkway in front of the University Church was built by the CPU High School Class of 1966 and, according to the university's official article, handed over to the university on January 4, 2003. A podium-like structure holds a marker unveiled on September 19, 1980 by the National Historical Institute (now the NHCP), so you can read the school's history at a glance.

It is the tallest building on campus and has long been its center. It is one of the buildings listed in the Philippine Registry of Heritage, so seeing it together with the Centennial Walkway is the basic route.

blocks.title: Stuart Hall and Old Valentine Hall

children.text: Stuart Hall, built in 1913–1914, is the oldest building on campus and was originally the principal's residence. Old Valentine Hall is named after the founder and now houses the College of Arts and Sciences and the College of Education.

blocks.title: Franklin Hall, Weston Hall and Roblee Science Hall

children.text: The dormitories and the science building face each other across the big field. These concrete buildings survived World War II, so they hint at the outline of the prewar campus.

blocks.title: Henry Luce III Library and the Hinilawod recordings

children.text: The library holds the recordings of the Panay oral epic that the Filipino anthropologist Felipe Landa Jocano made on his own tape recorder in 1956–1957, and they were inscribed in the UNESCO MOWCAP register in 2024. It also has the Meyer Asian Collection, a separate collection of Asian materials. However, no public viewing hours have been confirmed, so you should ask the library about access. According to CPU news, Jocano recorded the chanters Ulang Udig (Lambunao, Iloilo) and Narcisa "Hugan-an" Lingaya (Tapaz, Capiz). Hugan-an's recording took three weeks and runs about 30 hours. The inscription date was May 8, 2024.

According to the university, the campus has green spaces such as the Alumni Garden, the Half Moon and the University Botanical Garden. It is hot at midday, so walking in the early morning or around sunset is best.

blocks.title: Festival of Lights and Music at Central

children.text: The university and its alumni association hold this event during the Christmas season. According to the university's news, in 2024 it ran from December 6 to January 6, 2025, and in 2025 the lights were switched on on December 5. Check the university's official page or Facebook for this year's schedule. The event is run jointly by the CPU Alumni Association and the university, and the overall chairman for 2025 was introduced as Dr. Gleen A. M. Catedral. The switch-on location and program change a little every year, so check the announcement just before you go.

When most buildings were destroyed in World War II, the concrete-built Valentine Hall, Lopez Hall, Franklin Hall, Roblee Hall, Weston Hall and the President's House remained. Reading the information boards and working out which buildings stood before the war is a fun exercise.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: From Jaro Cathedral to the campus

children.text: Travel from downtown Iloilo to Jaro District by jeepney or taxi and have breakfast around the Jaro Cathedral plaza.
Let the gate staff know about your visit, then see the Centennial Walkway and the NHCP marker first.
Take photos in front of the University Church, then look at Old Valentine Hall and Stuart Hall, mostly from outside.
See Franklin Hall, Weston Hall and Roblee Science Hall across the big field, then walk toward the gardens.
Have lunch at a restaurant near the campus, then continue to Jaro Cathedral or downtown.

Many students pass through during class hours in the term, so do not enter buildings without permission. This schedule is mostly walking and does not include interiors. The campus is large, so seeing every building would take longer.
Arrive before sunset and see the area around the Centennial Walkway and the campus in daylight first.
Head to the lit areas at lighting time and enjoy the night view. Confirm the exact time locally.
When the crowd grows, leave early and catch a taxi or jeepney.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Airlines and timetables change often, so check before booking.
The airport is in Santa Barbara, away from downtown, and the trip into the city takes about
30–50 minutes
by van or taxi. Check current services locally.
Jaro District is close to the north of downtown Iloilo and can be reached by taxi or jeepney. Use Jaro Cathedral as a reference point and ask for CPU.
Taxi or Grab is convenient. Jeepney routes and fares change often, so check locally.
Jaro is a district of Iloilo City, so no long transfer is needed. You can also phone the university information center to ask for directions.
From other islands such as Cebu, take a ferry to Iloilo port and then a taxi or jeepney. Ask the shipping line for sailing times.
The dry season from November to May is good for walking. The period from early December to early January is especially lively at night because of the festival of lights.
In the rainy season from June to November, afternoon showers are frequent, so bring an umbrella. The campus mood varies with the school calendar and public holidays.

Iloilo is also famous for the Dinagyang Festival in late January, so if you combine the December festival of lights and January's Dinagyang in one trip, book your lodging early. Flights and rooms fill up fast during holidays.

Many visitors stay in hotels downtown or in and around Jaro District. The area around Jaro Cathedral is close to the campus, and staying in the downtown center makes it easy to combine with other Iloilo sights.

Iloilo is known for local dishes such as La Paz batchoy. There are many restaurants and cafes serving students around Jaro plaza and near the campus, so have lunch nearby. It is more accurate to check shop names locally.
The university hospital, CPU-Iloilo Mission Hospital, is also in Jaro District, which is a useful reference if you need nearby medical care. For evening events, plan your ride home in advance.
A weekday morning during the school term is the quietest time. For group visits, ask the university information center in advance.
The information center contact on the university's official site is infocenter@cpu.edu.ph and phone +63 33 329 1971.
Buildings hold classes and offices, so view them from outside and get permission before entering.
There are reports that the library's Meyer Asian Collection is not normally open to the public, so contact the library in advance if you want access.
There is little shade at midday, so bring a hat and water.
Combining it with Jaro Cathedral and Molo Church makes a full-day cultural route.
On evenings during the festival of lights, traffic is heavy, so arrive early or leave plenty of time when booking a Grab.
Besides this campus, Jaro District has other early-20th-century American colonial architecture, and comparing them on foot is fun. The Jaro Evangelical Church is one example.
This is a working university campus, so visiting rules and hours may change. Check the latest announcement before you go.
You may be asked about the purpose of your visit when entering, so please cooperate.
Move quietly so you do not disturb students or classes, and do not fly a drone without permission.
Watch for pickpockets in the festival crowds.
In the rainy season the paths are slippery and showers are frequent.
Follow local instructions on whether photography is allowed.
